questions.q: You buy a stock for ₹10,000 and sell it for ₹15,000 after 18 months. You also earned ₹500 in dividends. How much tax do you owe on this gain (ignoring any other income)?
options: Tax on ₹5,500 at your income tax slab rate (short-term capital gains)
Tax on ₹5,000 at 20% flat (long-term capital gains with indexation)
Tax on ₹5,500 at 20% flat (long-term capital gains without indexation)
No tax because gains under ₹1 lakh are exempt
questions.explain: After 18 months, it's long-term capital gains; indexation benefit applies, reducing the actual gain to ₹5,000, taxed at flat 20%; dividends are taxed separately as income.

questions.q: When the RBI raises the repo rate, what typically happens to bank lending rates and bond prices?
options: Bank lending rates rise, bond prices rise (better returns for savers)
Bank lending rates fall, bond prices fall (borrowing becomes cheaper)
Bank lending rates rise, bond prices fall (existing bond holders suffer mark-to-market losses)
Bank lending rates stay the same, bond prices fall (RBI controls both independently)
questions.explain: Higher repo rate increases banks' cost of funds, so they raise lending rates; new bonds with higher yields become more attractive, making older lower-yield bonds less valuable and their prices drop.

questions.q: If inflation is 6% per year and your fixed deposit earns 5%, what is your real return, and what does this mean?
options: Real return is 11%; your purchasing power increases by 11%
Real return is 1%; you lose 1% in purchasing power each year
Real return is -1%; your money is worth less even though the FD balance grows
Real return cannot be calculated without knowing GDP growth
questions.explain: Real return = nominal return minus inflation = 5% − 6% = −1%; even though your ₹100 grows nominally, it buys less stuff because prices rose faster than your interest earned.

questions.q: You buy a Nifty 50 call option with a strike of ₹20,000 for a premium of ₹200. If Nifty closes at ₹20,300 on expiry, what is your profit or loss (ignoring brokerage)?
options: Profit of ₹100 (you exercised the option and sold at ₹20,300)
Profit of ₹100 (intrinsic value ₹300 minus premium ₹200)
Loss of ₹200 (the option expires out of the money)
Profit of ₹300 (difference between strike and closing price)
questions.explain: At expiry, intrinsic value = ₹20,300 − ₹20,000 = ₹300; subtract the premium paid (₹200) to get net profit of ₹100; buying the option caps your loss to the premium regardless of how far the price falls.

questions.q: During an IPO, a company offers shares at ₹50 per share. On the first day of listing, the price jumps to ₹75. Who benefits from this price jump, and why might it happen?
options: The company benefits because it can issue more shares at the higher price
IPO investors (allottees) benefit; demand exceeded supply or the offer price was set too low by underwriters
No one really benefits; it's just random market noise and corrects within days
Secondary market traders benefit because volatility creates trading opportunities
questions.explain: Investors allotted shares at ₹50 can immediately sell at ₹75, locking in ₹25 profit; the company received ₹50 per share already during IPO and doesn't benefit from the post-listing jump; underpricing or strong demand causes the jump.
